S_how.S1: I imagined the words UK English speakers would probably write for each smell, guessed their word-pleasantness scores (pulled in toward the middle because they are averages), and did not use the 24 example values, because they do not follow the smells' pleasantness (for example, cadaver 6.90 and soap 6.74 but fresh bread 4.29) and so look unreliable as a guide.
S_how.S2: I estimated how pleasant the words people would typically use for each smell are, keeping to the roughly 3.1 to 7.1 range of the examples, but I did not follow the examples' pattern, because many look inverted (dead animal, cadaver, rotten meat, dumpsite, compost and barnyard high; shampoo, body lotion, fresh bread and lily low), so I relied on the obvious pleasant/unpleasant split instead.
S_how.S3: I guessed the typical word-valence of descriptions for each smell (pleasant about 6.5, unpleasant about 4) and then shrank those guesses strongly toward the reference mean of 5.47, because the 24 reference values (e.g. cadaver 6.90, soap 6.74 vs shampoo 3.40, fresh bread 4.29) show essentially no relation to how pleasant the smell is.
S_how.S4: I estimated each value from how pleasant the smell typically is and how pleasant the words people usually use for it would score on an English word-valence list, compressed toward the middle of the scale; the 24 example values did not follow a pleasantness pattern I could use (e.g. cadaver 6.90, shampoo 3.40), so I did not fit to them.
S_how.S5: I estimated how pleasant the words people typically use for each smell would be, then pulled every estimate strongly toward the anchor average of about 5.5 because the 24 given examples (e.g. cadaver 6.90, dumpsite 6.47, fresh bread 4.29, shampoo 3.40) show almost no relation to how pleasant the smells actually are.
S_how.S6: I estimated each value from how pleasant the words people would likely use for that smell are on a typical 1-9 word-valence list, and set the range from the T examples' plausible values (about 3.3 for foul smells to about 7 for pleasant ones), not copying their pattern, because many examples looked reversed (e.g. dead animal 6.63, cadaver 6.90, shampoo 3.40, body lotion 3.34).
